layer0_index.description: Iron Arrow's Law School era, lawyer chiefs, and Henry King Stanford.
layer0_index.one_sentence_summary: Section Four: Law School Domination: Iron Arrow's Law School era, lawyer chiefs, and Henry King Stanford. (5 subsections)

layer1_summary.paragraph: The Law School era represents a pivotal chapter in Iron Arrow's institutional history, during which the society's leadership and ceremonial presence became deeply intertwined with the University of Miami's physical and administrative landscape. This section traces how a succession of lawyer chiefs shaped Iron Arrow's governance while figures like Henry King Stanford helped secure the society's symbolic place at the heart of campus.
bullets: John Leatherwood, who became Chief in 1969, played a central role in rescuing the vandalized tribal membership plaques from the student union breezeway and overseeing the creation of the new large arrow-shaped plaque that would become Iron Arrow's enduring physical symbol.

The idea for the giant copper arrow-shaped plaque originated with Freddy Morris and was developed in collaboration with Thurston Adams, representing a generational handoff of stewardship over Iron Arrow's material heritage.

Chief Leatherwood negotiated directly with University of Miami President Henry King Stanford to secure cabinet approval for placing the Iron Arrow plaques alongside the Ashe statue in the Ashe Administration Building, a placement the cabinet had initially rejected.

The rededication of the Ashe Building at Homecoming 1970, with Iron Arrow presiding alongside the statue of founder Bowman Foster Ashe and the tribal membership plaques, cemented the society's foundational identity within the university's official spaces.

Running beneath the political and ceremonial victories of this era is a broader cultural anxiety about the destruction of South Florida's natural landscape, which the text connects to Iron Arrow's spiritual roots in the Florida wilderness.

layer2_details.text:
AN IRON ARROW ELECTION

- Source of plaque history: Thurston Adams's letter to the author, dated July 4, 1974
- Adams discovered and retrieved the original shield-shaped Iron Arrow plaque from a pile of rubble slated for discard
- First location after retrieval: south side, ground floor of the Merrick Building ("the 'Old Skeleton'"), described as "First Society, First Structure" — the original intended entirety of UM in the 1920s
- Second location: wall of the Memorial Building, placed to one side and behind the bronze statue of Dr. Ashe, facing the Lecture Hall; Adams quote: "And there for years, it stayed on the wall facing the Lecture Hall in the Memorial Building close by its founder."
- A second, rectangular bronze plaque was added during the Memorial Building years to accommodate new members' names
- Third location: breezeway entrance of the Student Union, where both the old shield-shaped plaque and the rectangular copper plaque were moved when the Student Union was built
- Freddy Morris originated the idea for a large arrow-shaped plaque; Adams recounts the exchange: Morris asked what Adams was thinking, Adams said he was figuring out size and placement; Morris said, "Doc, why don't you have a big copper arrow that you could engrave the members' names on for years?"; Adams replied, "Freddy, Goddamn! That's a wonderful idea! And I will do just that, provided, of course, the society approves." The society approved.
- Footnote 103 cites: Adams, Thurston, letter to the author, July 4, 1974
- Adams retired after 21 years of service at the University, retiring to Turkey Creek Lodge in Pine Apple, Alabama (his boyhood home) before he could carry out the arrow-plaque idea
- Plaques remained in the Student Union breezeway only one year after Adams left
- John Leatherwood became Chief in 1969; vandalism and lewd scarring had damaged the plaques, making it his task to execute the concept Adams and Morris had conceived
- William Vaught suggested the old shield-shaped plaque form the center section of the large arrow's shaft
- A full-scale cardboard mock-up was made from these ideas and delivered with specifications to a local foundry
- The completed giant arrow plaque was cast in four pieces
- Leatherwood refused to place the plaque again in the breezeway; he stored all four pieces in his apartment in the 960 dormitory complex
- Leatherwood approached UM Vice President Eugene Cohen about moving the Ashe Statue to the lobby of the Ashe Building, with the arrow-shaped plaques placed adjacent
- Cohen presented the proposal to the University cabinet; cabinet approved relocation of the statue but initially rejected adjacent placement of the Iron Arrow plaques
- Leatherwood made an appointment with Dr. Stanford (president) to secure his personal sponsorship before the cabinet; he arrived carrying all four large, heavy plaques under his arms
- With Dr. Stanford's support, based on the historical relationship between Dr. Ashe and Iron Arrow, cabinet approval was quickly granted
- Fourth and final location: lobby of the Ashe Administration Building, alongside the Ashe statue and the tribal membership plaques
- Official rededication of the Ashe Building occurred at Homecoming, 1970, presided over by Iron Arrow

BITS AND PIECES

- Jerry Herman was famous at the University of Miami in the early 1950s
- Herman became an Iron Arrow member in 1954–55 as a result of a musical production called "Sketchbook," which he wrote and had performed in the University's old, makeshift box theatre
- By 1975, Herman's Broadway hits included "Milk and Honey," "Mame," and "Hello, Dolly!"; "Hello, Dolly!" was described as the second longest-running Broadway musical of all time
- On November 5, 1975, Herman was Grand Marshal of the Homecoming Parade and special guest at President Stanford's Iron Arrow Reception
- November 6, 1975: his concert in the university's new Gusman Hall was a sellout; Herman told his audience, "This is better than any opening night I've ever had."
- November 7, 1975: the UM Drama Department named Herman the first Founding Member of its Hall of Fame
- November 8, 1975: President Stanford presented Herman with the Alumnus of Distinction Award at the Annual Dinner Dance
- 1960 survey by Edwin Smith found: more than 6 percent of Iron Arrow members hold political offices; 17 percent hold posts in universities and colleges; 23 percent are business executives (bank presidents, heads of large firms, editors)
- Iron Arrow members who went on to professional football: George Mira (San Francisco 49ers); Ted Hendricks (Baltimore Colts and Oakland Raiders); Chuck Foreman, 1973 rookie-of-the-year (Minnesota Vikings); Burgess Owens (New York Jets); Rubin Carter (Denver Broncos); Dennis Harrah (Los Angeles Rams); Tony Cline (Oakland Raiders); Walt Kichefski (Pittsburgh Steelers); Don Bosseler (Washington Redskins); Thomas Kearns (New York Giants and Chicago Cardinals); additional members: Tom Beier, Fran Curci, Frank McDonald, Al Carapella, Bill Miller, Eddie Dunn
- Basketball: All-American Rick Barry, later with the Golden State Warriors, was an Iron Arrow member (while UM still had basketball)
- Baseball: Al Rosen went on to the Cleveland Indians; Ron Fraser was named Head Coach of the 1971 U.S. team at the Pan American Games
- Tennis: Gardner Mulloy, Ed Rubinoff, and Jaime Fillol won international fame
- Swimming: Jack Nelson was named Olympic Swimming Coach for the U.S. Women's team at the 1976 Olympics
- Prior to 1965, most Iron Arrow members did not own their own Seminole jackets; tribally owned jackets were borrowed for tapping ceremonies and returned afterward; tactful reminders were sometimes necessary to retrieve them
